# Akittijātaka (Ja 480)

**ID:** Ja 480
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Akittijātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul12.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Akittijātaka* (Ja 480) is a birth story of the Bodhisatta recounting his life as the wealthy brāhmaṇa Akitti of Benares, identified with the sage Agastya and also addressed by the family name Kassapa [Speyer 1895; Mein Da 2015]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana in connection with a generous donor living in Sāvatthī [Fausböll 1887]. Seeking renunciation, Akitti distributed his immense riches, departed Benares through what became remembered as the Akitti Gate (*Akittidvāra*) and Akitti Ferry (*Akittitittha*), and entered the ascetic life accompanied initially by his sister [Fausböll 1887; Mein Da 2015]. He later developed meditative insight in a garden at Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam before retreating to supreme solitude on Ahidīpa (subsequently known as Karadīpa, near Nāgadīpa off northern Sri Lanka), subsisting solely on kara-leaves sprinkled with water [Adikaram 1946; Monius 2001; Mein Da 2015].

Akitti's austere tapas heated the heavenly throne of Sakka, who visited him in the guise of a brāhmaṇa mendicant to test his detachment [Sahni 2008; Mein Da 2015]. Akitti joyfully offered his meagre food to the visitor for three consecutive days without keeping any for himself [Sahni 2008]. When an impressed Sakka offered him boons, the ascetic rejected all worldly desires, requesting instead spiritual blessings such as never being subjected to the sight, sound, or company of a fool, and remaining free from anger, greed, and insatiability [Anandajoti 2010; Speyer 1895]. Akitti's sacrifice is celebrated across canonical and post-canonical literature—such as the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and *Jātakanidānakathā*—as a prime embodiment of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) [Appleton 2010; Gaffney 2003].

**Sources**

- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 Verses from the Canon (2010) — Detailed the ascetic's boon request regarding not associating with fools.
- [Sahni 2008] Pragati Sahni, Environmental Ethics in Buddhism: A Virtues Approach (2008) — Provided details on Akitti's renunciation and three-day almsgiving to Sakka.
- [Adikaram 1946] E. W. Adikaram, Early History of Buddhism in Ceylon (1946) — Provided geographical identification of Ahidīpa / Karadīpa near Nāgadīpa.
- [Monius 2001] Anne E. Monius, Imagining a Place for Buddhism: Literary Culture and Religious Community in Tamil-Speaking South India (2001) — Noted the setting of Akitti's meditative retreat in Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Documented the citation of Akitti in the Cariyāpiṭaka's verse on dānapāramī.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with Its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Provided the Pali commentary opening and narrative details of Akitti's departure from Benares.
- [Speyer 1895] J. S. Speyer (tr.), The Jātakamālā: Garland of Birth-Stories of Āryaśūra (1895) — Noted the identification of Akitti with Agastya and Kassapa, and Sakka's boon dialogues.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Referenced the Bodhisatta's perfection of pāramīs in the time of Akitti.
- [Mein Da 2015] Ashin War Yar Mein Da, Pāramīs/Pāramitās in Theravāda and Mahāyāna (2015) — Provided narrative summary regarding Akitti as a magnate of Benares and his ascetic life on Karadīpa.
